answer:
Hormozi would tell you to raise your prices, and so would I. Taking on more clients at your current price adds work without fixing what's actually limiting you.

**Why Hormozi says raise prices:**

1. **In a service business, you raise prices.** In his "Mathematics of Business" episode, he says raising prices is almost always the right move. The main exception is something that scales without limit, like software. A service business runs out of people's time before it runs out of demand, so "there's only one way you go in service which is up." He says higher prices give you better margins, a better reputation, and the money to hire better people. A 4-person agency is limited by its team's hours. Every client you add at today's price uses up hours you've already sold too cheaply.

2. **Small price increases have a big effect on profit.** In one case study he worked out that "10% price raise for you equals roughly a 25% increase in net profit." In a Q&A he said "pricing is the strongest lever that you have on making money." He also said that if you double your price, you can lose 25% of your conversions and still come out ahead. Another podcast describes one of his portfolio companies: he pushed a 50% price increase on a CEO who resisted, changed nothing else, and profit tripled within three months.

3. **Clients who pay more do better.** He argues that a higher price makes clients more convinced you can deliver and more invested in the work. Invested clients get better results, and better results make retention easier. That matters a lot for an agency.

4. **Your close rate tells you how far to go.** These are his rules of thumb:
   - 80% or more: you're 3–4x underpriced
   - 60–80%: 2–3x
   - 50–60%: 1.5–2x
   - 40–50%: 1.25–1.5x
   - 30–40%: about right, assuming your sales process educates buyers before the pitch
   - Under 30%: the problem is targeting or sales, not price

**What to do:**
- Look at your close rate on your last 10–20 sales calls and use the bands above to set your new price for incoming clients.
- Raise prices on current clients by a smaller amount, something like 10–20%. In the same Q&A he warned that churn tends to rise after a price increase, and churn is what kills a retainer business. Check your numbers: losing one or two of your lowest-value clients is fine. Your monthly churn doubling is not.
- Use the hours you free up to get better results for the clients who stay. Only add clients once your margin can cover hiring good people to serve them.

My own rough math, not Hormozi's: $35k a month across 4 people is about $105k a year per head. That's thin for an agency once you take out salaries. A 20% price increase that costs you one or two clients probably leaves you with more profit and less work than signing three new clients at your current rate.

One caveat: I found no Hormozi quote aimed specifically at small agencies. Everything above is his general service-business advice, and most of it comes from auto-generated podcast transcripts and third-party summaries, so the exact wording may be slightly off.

**Spend it on paid ads and answer the calls yourself. Hire a salesperson later.**

I couldn't find a place where Hormozi compares these two options directly, so this pick is my reading of what he's said elsewhere. Those statements point the same way:

1. **He says local businesses are the easiest to advertise.** In his "8 Ad Strategies for 8 Different Businesses" episode, he says "local businesses are the easiest business to run ads for" and that local ads are "very offer driven." His suggestion for a small local practice was a cheap starter offer, "the $19 to $99 thing," not a sales hire. For a home-services business (roofing), he said that if the ads pay back well, you should "spend more."
2. **He tells small owners to do the selling themselves.** His advice to the same local business was: "You still call all the leads yourself." A salesperson with no leads has nothing to sell, and right now the $10k is mainly a way to get leads.
3. **He says to hire once the work is more than you can handle.** In the "Employees and Agencies" section of *$100M Leads*, he says "in due time, it will take more work than a single person can handle." At that point you hire people who "get you leads the exact same way you got your own leads," using a checklist you've already written ("Step one, document"). You can't write that checklist until you've done the selling yourself.
4. **The numbers point the same way.** $10k covers only a few months of a salesperson's pay, and Hormozi pays well (one summary says around the 90th percentile). The same $10k in ads gets you real data on cost per lead and close rate.

**How to do it the Hormozi way:**
- Lead with an offer that's hard to say no to, like a discounted first deep clean that turns into a recurring service. Don't just advertise "cleaning services."
- Make sure the first month of ads is mainly for learning. A third-party summary of his ads teaching describes a "data acquisition" phase where you spend before you're profitable. Keep a little money aside for retargeting.
- Track what it costs you to win a customer and what that customer is worth over time. The same summary says he aims for lifetime gross profit of at least 3x that cost.
- Call every lead within minutes, write down what works, and hire a salesperson once you're missing calls.

One caveat: a newsletter writer notes that Hormozi has recently been "steering away from paid ads" for his own business. That's about his own content-driven brand, though. For a local service business, his advice above still says ads.

**Cut it down. Hormozi's answer is close to explicit: don't add more workouts and content, take things away and make what's left better.**

**What he said**

In a talk on keeping customers, transcribed and attributed to him on SozAI, he says:

- **Overwhelm is the main reason people cancel.** "The number one reason people churn, outside of price, is overwhelm." Members think "I don't have the time, I can't keep up, I can't utilize it."
- **Unused content makes the program feel worse value.** "When you have five things that you pay for, but you only use one, you feel like you're only getting 20% of the value." Each workout a member skips becomes a reason to cancel.
- **The fix is subtraction.** "We need to fix them through subtraction and amelioration, aka making it better rather than adding more stuff." And: "If you can only do one thing that gets people to stay, why would you do five?"
- **Value per second.** "Think about value per second, not seconds of value." Busy members want the most results from the least time.

This also fits his value equation: perceived value goes up when effort and time delay go down. A bigger content library adds effort, so it lowers value.

**What he'd tell you to do**

1. **Cut to one clear weekly rhythm.** Something like three set workouts a week and one check-in. Keep extra material as optional depth for your most committed members, not as the main program.
2. **Get new members a quick win in their first day.** He says month one is when the most people cancel, so put that quick win right at the start.
3. **Make results visible by about day 90, and build community by month six.** In this talk he says that by around month six, whether people stay depends mostly on their connections with other members.
4. **Ask everyone who cancels why.** Look for patterns. If you hear "I couldn't keep up," that confirms the overwhelm problem.
5. **Lower the cost of staying.** Offer a pause option instead of only cancel, and offer annual plans, so people decide once rather than every month.

One caveat: the direct quotes come from a third-party transcript of a Hormozi talk. I couldn't find the original video to check them against, though they match his published frameworks.

**Keep the 9-to-5 for now.** Quit only when your business can replace your paycheck. This is Hormozi's own advice, even though he quit his consulting job to start a gym.

**What he says**

In *The Game* Ep 525, "From Side Hustle to Main Hustle," he gives three conditions to meet before you quit:
1. **About six months of living expenses saved.** "Six months of living, is what I would feel comfortable with before starting my next thing." If you have a family, you need more.
2. **The business at least matches your salary.** "I need my side hustle to at least match my income from my current role." If you only have a few hours a week, ask whether your full working week would get you there: "If I had the other 36 hours back to add to my four, would I be able to match that?"
3. **That income lasts.** One good month doesn't count. "I want to sustain that level of income for six months."

He also says to live below your means on your job income alone. He calls going from a job to paying yourself "the single hardest jump in all of entrepreneurship." Nowhere in that episode does he say to burn the boats. His approach is to take risk out before you commit fully.

In Ep 312, "When to Start a Business," he calls quitting "the hardest entrepreneurial decision of my entire life." He says he only did it because he was miserable. He suggests trying lower-risk options first: change employers, find a job that pays you to learn, or build the business on the side. Quit only once you have savings, a business model you've tested, and proof that other people are succeeding with the same thing. He also warns that your income will probably drop for several years after you leave.

**Two caveats he'd add**
- The side business has to be the main hustle in the making. If you just want extra money, he calls that "a distraction from what your real main hustle is." Treat your job as a place to learn skills your business will use.
- Building on the side will mean a "season of sacrifice": nights and weekends, with less time for family and hobbies. That's the cost of not betting everything.

Leila Hormozi gives the same advice on her podcast: get a paying client before you quit and know your real financial floor. She also cites research finding that founders who kept their day jobs were 33% less likely to fail. I got that point from an episode summary, not a transcript.

**What to do:** Keep the job and cut your expenses. Put every spare hour into the business. Hand in your notice once it has matched your salary for six months and you have six months of savings. Until then, quitting is a gamble, and Hormozi's advice is to reduce the risk first.

I've finished researching, so here's the answer.

## Pick the guarantee, but make it conditional, not unconditional

Of your two options, Hormozi would steer you away from a strict no-refunds policy. He also wouldn't recommend a plain "money back if you're not happy" guarantee. For a $2,000 coaching program he'd tell you to use a **conditional guarantee**: the client gets their money back (or more) only if they did the work and still didn't get the result.

**Why not no-refunds:** His "anti-guarantee" ("all sales are final") is meant for products that "massively diminish in value when used," where "once seen can't be unseen." Think consumables or information the buyer keeps forever. Coaching is an ongoing service that depends on the client doing the work, so that reasoning doesn't fit well. He also argues that "reversing risk is the number one way to increase conversion of an offer." By refusing refunds you give that up.

**Why not an unconditional refund either:** He describes unconditional guarantees as "basically a trial where they pay first and see if they like it." He says "the higher the ticket, the more business oriented it is, the more you want to steer towards specific guarantees," and that broad guarantees suit low-ticket consumer offers. He also warns that "people who buy because of guarantees can become very shitty customers." His fix is to "tie the guarantee to their efforts."

**Why guaranteeing more still pays:** His example: if a stronger guarantee lets you close 130% more people and refunds double from 5% to 10%, "you still make 23 percent more." He also says "even if you make a crazy guarantee, most people won't take advantage of it."

## What it could look like

> "Attend every weekly call, complete every assignment, and submit your numbers each week. If you haven't hit [specific result] in 90 days, I'll keep coaching you free until you do. Or, if you'd rather, I'll refund your $2,000."

- **"Keep working for free" (service guarantee):** This is one of his favorites. He says "I have yet to have a single person say a client took them up on it." Put a limit on the extra time, roughly twice the original program length, so you aren't "on hook forever."
- **Stacking:** If you want an easier entry point, add a short unconditional window (for example, a full refund within 14 days) on top of the conditional 90-day guarantee. He says "you can actually stack guarantees."
- **How to present it:** "You must hit your guarantee hard… say it bold and give the reason why." Put it in the pitch itself, not in the fine print.

**A caveat on sources:** I couldn't access the book's text directly. The quotes above come from a podcast transcript page and reader notes on *$100M Offers*, so exact wording may differ a little from the book.

**My recommendation, based on Hormozi's public advice: pay off the credit cards first and get rid of the car payment. Keep 3–6 months of living expenses in cash. Only the money left after that should go into the business, and only into things you've already seen pay back.**

I couldn't find a clip where Hormozi answers this exact question, so this is pieced together from what he has said. Here's why it points that way:

1. **He tells people to clear their fixed payments before investing.** In his "30x12" money advice, he says to turn in a car lease and "buy a $5,000 car." He describes a $600/month payment as "working six of your 22 days for the car that you drive to work with." His view is that once you don't have a car payment or a mortgage, you're free to go "all in on investments." His own story is about using the savings from dropping a car payment to pay down debt, and he calls watching that debt shrink "so reinforcing." ([Financial Anarchy summary](https://financialanarchy.substack.com/p/unlock-your-millionaire-potential))

2. **He wants a cash cushion before you take risks.** He recommends 3–6 months of expenses in an interest-bearing account, because "your level of anxiety around everything else in life will go down." ([same source](https://financialanarchy.substack.com/p/unlock-your-millionaire-potential)) If you put your entire $50k into the business, you'd still have the debt payments and no cushion, which is the opposite of what he describes.

3. **"Invest in yourself" is about skills, not handing cash to a business.** He told Dave Ramsey, "You're always going to get higher returns on investing in your own education, your own skill sets, compared to any stock market." His examples were cheap ones, like a roughly $500 certification that could triple someone's income. ([Ramsey Show transcript](https://podscripts.co/podcasts/the-ramsey-show-app/alex-hormozi-dont-take-poor-peoples-advice-on-getting-rich-hour-1), [Yahoo Finance](https://finance.yahoo.com/news/sadness-ignorance-first-generation-iranian-100000901.html)) Write-ups of his business teaching make a related point: marketing spend doesn't fix a weak offer, it "amplifies it." ([Indie Hackers](https://www.indiehackers.com/post/founders-story-why-alex-hormozi-says-your-business-doesn-t-have-a-marketing-problem-3aae92da5e))

4. **The math agrees.** Paying off a card that charges about 20% interest is a guaranteed 20% return ([Bankrate](https://www.bankrate.com/personal-finance/debt/what-debt-should-you-pay-off-first), [Investor.gov](https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/investing-basics/save-and-invest/pay-credit-cards-or-other-high-interest)). Very few early-stage businesses reliably beat that.

**What to do:**
- **Credit cards:** pay them off today, highest interest rate first.
- **Car:** if it's expensive, sell it and buy a cheap used car with cash, which is his $5,000-car advice. If it's already modest, pay off the loan.
- **Emergency fund:** set aside 3–6 months of expenses.
- **Business:** put the rest here, in small amounts, into specific things with measurable returns, like an ad test, a skill, or a better offer. Add more only after they pay back.

**One exception:** if the business already makes money and you can show that each dollar you put in comes back well above 20% (for example, ads with a proven cost to acquire a customer), Hormozi's "skills beat the market" reasoning would favor funding it. Even then, pay off the credit cards first.

A note on the sources: the most direct quotes come from the Ramsey Show transcript and Yahoo Finance. The car and emergency-fund advice comes from a secondhand Substack summary, and the "amplifies" point is from an Indie Hackers write-up, so neither is a verbatim transcript.

I'd make long-form YouTube videos the core of your content and cut short clips out of them. Don't build the business on clips alone. That's the answer that best matches what Hormozi has said and done, although most of what I found is other people reporting his views, not his own transcripts.

**Why long-form, in his reasoning:**

1. **Short clips get you seen, but they don't get people to trust you.** In a podcast recap, Hormozi is quoted as saying: *"Short-form content does not build tremendous influence. It can bring awareness, but not deep influence."* He reportedly estimates that about 10 hours of 20–30 minute videos does as much as roughly 1,800 twenty-second clips. He names four things that build influence, all easier to show in long videos: being liked, credibility, power and status. ([Karat](https://news.trykarat.com/p/future-of-short-form-content))
2. **Long-form is where his sales came from.** One write-up quotes him saying *"Long-form drove the book sales, the email opt-ins and the applications to join Acquisition.com's portfolio."* It also says the people who watch Shorts mostly don't go on to watch long videos: *"Shorts viewers want more shorts. Long-form viewers want more longs."* That's the one exception he allows: someone can find you through a clip on one platform and then watch your long videos somewhere else. ([Postiz](https://postiz.com/blog/hormozi-2026-audience-growth-playbook))
3. **He judges content by audience quality, not views.** He reportedly switched his main metric from views to RPM, YouTube's ad revenue per thousand views, as a measure of whether he's reaching the right people. A test that made his videos more entertaining roughly doubled or tripled views but halved ad revenue. ([Postiz](https://postiz.com/blog/hormozi-2026-audience-growth-playbook))

**What his channel actually does:** One analytics site says about 99% of his recent uploads are long-form, averaging around 40 minutes ([OutlierKit channel page](https://outlierkit.com/channel/alexhormozi)). A separate teardown says about 91% of his views still come from Shorts, which are mostly cut from his long talks and podcasts ([OutlierKit strategy teardown](https://outlierkit.com/resources/alex-hormozi-growth-strategy/)). So he records the long piece once and cuts it into many clips ([Watsspace](https://watsspace.com/blog/alex-hormozis-marketing-strategy/)). In other words, clips are for reach and long-form is for turning viewers into customers.

**What to do:**
- Publish one useful long video every week, 20 minutes or more, on a problem your buyers actually have.
- Cut 5–10 clips from each one and post them everywhere. Treat them as a way to get discovered and to test which hooks work, not as the main event.
- Measure success by email sign-ups, booked calls and sales. Don't measure it by views.
- Give much more than you ask for. In his podcast he suggests about 3 value pieces for every ask in long-form, and far fewer asks in short-form, about 1 promotional post in 11 ([Shortform summary of ep. 892](https://www.shortform.com/podcast/episode/the-game-w-alex-hormozi-2025-05-23-episode-summary-give-more-ask-less-ep-892)).

**Caveat:** These are blogs, newsletters and analytics sites summarizing him. Some are selling content tools, and none gives exact video titles or dates for these quotes. The closest thing to a primary source is his podcast episode "The Content Accordion" (ep. 845). I could only read its first few minutes ([Audioscrape](https://audioscrape.com/podcast/the-game-with-alex-hormozi/episode/my-approach-to-scalable-content---the-content-accordion--ep-845)), so listen to the full episode if you want it in his own words.

**Keep full price.** Run a Black Friday sale anyway, but make the deal a stack of bonuses that disappear at a deadline, not 30% off. That's the most direct reading of what Hormozi has written.

**What he has said**

In the *$100M Offers* material (from a transcript of his own audiobook reading), he's blunt about discounting your main product:
- "Add bonuses instead of discounting whenever possible on core offers."
- "Whenever trying to close a deal, never discount the main offer."
- Why: "It teaches your customers that your prices are negotiable, which is terrible." Adding bonuses "puts you in a position of strength and goodwill rather than weakness."

He also says the urgency should sit on the bonuses, not the price: "If you buy today, I will add in XYZ bonus that normally costs $1,000 for free… I want to reward action takers." People who wait lose the bonuses, but the price never changes.

**How to apply it to your Black Friday**

1. Keep the course at full price.
2. Add 2–4 bonuses that each remove one objection buyers have about your course. Examples: a live Q&A call, templates, a "first 30 days" quick-start, or a cohort or community slot. Give each one a benefit-driven name and a stated dollar value. Summaries of his bonus chapter describe naming and pricing bonuses this way.
3. Set a hard deadline, like Friday through Cyber Monday, and actually remove the bonuses afterward. Where you can, limit the numbers too ("20 seats on the live call").
4. Pick bonuses that cost you little to deliver. Third-party math shows why: a 20% discount on an $85 item gives up $17 on every sale, while a bundled add-on cost about $3.

**If you really want a price cut**

Summaries of his newer "Discount Promotions" material (*$100M Lost Chapters* and *Money Models*) suggest steep discounts belong on related or entry-level items, not the core offer. So discount a smaller add-on or use it as a lead-in, and keep the course price intact.

**Caveats**

I didn't find anything where Hormozi talks about Black Friday by name. This answer applies his general rule on discounts vs. bonuses to your situation. The direct quotes come from a transcript of his *$100M Offers* audiobook. The "Discount Promotions" point is a third-party summary I couldn't verify against the book.

**Hire the experienced manager from outside, and keep your best rep selling.** I couldn't find Hormozi addressing this exact choice directly, so that pick is my reading of what he has said nearby. Most of what I found is secondhand summaries of his podcasts and posts, not his own words.

**What points to an outside hire:**

1. **Closing and coaching are different skills.** A summary of his sales-training content says "Your best salesperson might not be the best manager" and "Closing deals and coaching are different skills." In that material, a manager needs "patience, leadership, and a desire to develop others" and should be fine with reps eventually outperforming them. Most star closers are wired the other way. ([notes](https://naveens-organization-10.gitbook.io/naveennotes/alex-hormozi-notes/sales-mindset-multiplier-and-sales-training-by-alex-hormozis))
2. **The manager matters more than the team.** A Threads post attributed to him says people leave managers, not jobs, and to hire great managers before great teams because the team follows the leader. ([Threads](https://www.threads.com/@hormozi/post/DdC7JuQoAx_/the-simplest-explanation-for-hiring-a-team-you-can-outwork-anyone-but-you-cant/)) Choosing the leader is the biggest lever you have, so don't fill the job by default.
3. **He seems to have done it himself.** A listing for his interview with Daniel G says that when he scaled a 40-person sales team, he first brought in an exceptional sales director and treated that role as a "sales operator." ([audio](https://audio.com/ffone-podcast/audio/hormozi-daniel-g-greatest-sales-interview)) I only saw this in a search snippet; the page itself blocked me.
4. **The job is mostly coaching.** In his "$100M Sales Teams" material, managers listen to call recordings, give regular feedback, run role-plays, keep leaderboards and KPIs, and are willing to cut the bottom 10%. **Double down on the first business. Hormozi's answer would be no second business line, at least not yet.**

**Why he'd say that, based on what I found:**

1. **More, then Better, then New, in that order.** Hormozi says that once you've found your highest-leverage activity, you first do more of what already works, then make it work better, and only after that try something new: *"Once we do all the mores and all the betters, then and only then do we do New."* He says most owners reach for "New" first, and that chasing a silver bullet is what's "killing most of you guys." A second business line is about as "New" as it gets. At $1M a year you almost certainly haven't run out of "More" or "Better" (more leads, faster lead response, better offer, higher price, better conversion).

2. **He made this exact mistake himself.** In his Future Flipper keynote, he says he grew a supplement company to $26M a year and then added another revenue stream instead of growing the original. Total revenue reached about $37M, and he still calls that a strategic mistake. He'd learned to turn down $5–10M distractions, but not one the same size as his business. Another episode is titled "why creating another business isn't the answer." By the episode summaries, he says he can't be CEO of two businesses, and he regretted starting his second company, Prestige Labs.

3. **"The woman in the red dress."** That's his name for the shiny opportunity that pulls you off your main business, and he says it gets more tempting the bigger you get. His lines: *"You need to become the person who can say no to the woman in the red dress,"* and *"The ability to say no is the thing that grows it."*

4. **Focused competitors win.** *"Compete against somebody who's doing lots of things. It's very easy to win."* His estimate is that you only need about a tenth of their effort. *"When you focus on one thing, you make it unreasonable to fail."* His own proof is that he sold his gyms and closed his agencies to focus on Gym Launch. It went from zero to $1.5M a month in 12 months, and to $4.5M a month a year after that.

**What to do instead:** Write the second-business idea on an "ideas list" and park it. He reportedly keeps such a list (that comes from a secondhand summary). Then work through More and Better on the $1M business: find the constraint (leads, sales or fulfilment), fix it, and repeat. If an idea mainly helps your current customers, treat it as "Better" for the core business, not a new business. Only revisit "New" once more volume and better execution truly stop growing the business.

A caveat: the quotes come from transcript and summary sites, not Hormozi's own published writing. The "can't be CEO of two businesses" and Prestige Labs points come from episode blurbs only, because those episode pages returned 404 errors when I tried to open them.

I've finished searching (four of Hormozi's podcast transcripts). Here's the answer.

## Verdict: Keep it, unless the business is starting to decline or you have something bigger to put your time into.

He never addresses a "3x offer" directly, but his stated views point clearly toward keeping it.

**1. A 3x offer just pays you three years of profit up front, minus taxes and fees.** In "Why I Sold," Hormozi says he's generally been anti-sale. His reasoning: a sale lowers your after-tax net worth because of transaction costs and taxes, while equity you keep goes on compounding. At 3x the buyer earns their money back in about three years and owns everything after that. If you keep it, you collect those three years yourself and still own the business. ([Ep 372](https://podscripts.co/podcasts/the-game-with-alex-hormozi/why-i-sold-ep-372))

**2. 3x is a normal price, not a great one.** He says most small businesses sell for roughly 1–3x because they aren't very reliable. Businesses under $5M in profit average about 3.75x, and institutional buyers pay a median of about 6.7x. So this offer is at or slightly below what's typical. It isn't the kind of premium that makes giving up the cash flow obviously worth it. ([Ep 493](https://podscripts.co/podcasts/the-game-with-alex-hormozi/how-to-sell-a-business-ep-493), [Ep 350](https://podscripts.co/podcasts/the-game-with-alex-hormozi/how-to-sell-your-business-ep-350))

**3. "Rich people only sell when they think the party's over."** He sold his own companies (a $46.2M valuation) for one reason: he wanted his time and focus back for one bigger business. He says the money itself didn't matter to him. ([Ep 372](https://podscripts.co/podcasts/the-game-with-alex-hormozi/why-i-sold-ep-372))

## When he'd say sell
- **The business is flat or shrinking.** He says "most people sell too late" and "very few people sell too early." Buyers pay for growth, and once a business declines, they back away. ([Ep 493](https://podscripts.co/podcasts/the-game-with-alex-hormozi/how-to-sell-a-business-ep-493))
- **You have a clearly bigger opportunity** and this business is taking up the focus you need for it. That's the "opportunity cost of my headspace" reason he gave for his own sale.

## What to do with the offer
- **Use it as leverage.** He says "you want to have a business you don't want to sell," because "you win negotiations before you start them by having options."
- **Fix what keeps the price low before you think about selling again.** That means customer concentration, depending on you personally, one sales channel, and no repeatable sales process. Then show 12–18 months of growth. That's how a business moves from 3x toward the higher multiples. ([Ep 493](https://podscripts.co/podcasts/the-game-with-alex-hormozi/how-to-sell-a-business-ep-493))
- **If you do negotiate, decide your walk-away number in advance.** Also check how much is actually paid in cash at closing. Seller financing, earnouts and escrow can mean you receive much less than the headline "3x." (Same episode.)

# Build it yourself with AI tools, but first make sure the app fixes your biggest problem

I couldn't find anywhere that Hormozi answers "vibe-code it or hire a developer" directly. Most of what's below comes from third-party summaries of his 2026 episodes, not transcripts. Still, his stated views point clearly to one answer: **learn to build the first version yourself.** Here's why he'd say that.

**1. First, check that the app is your bottleneck.** On *Diary of a CEO* (July 2026) he described a company that spent $350,000 building an AI system to replace 11 virtual assistants cleaning data, when its real problem was getting customers: "They still need more customers. That wasn't the thing." He says most entrepreneurs automate processes that are not "the binding constraint on their growth." If your app doesn't fix your biggest growth problem, his answer is neither option. Don't build it yet.

**2. If it is the bottleneck, he'd want you to learn it, not hand it off.** In Ep. 968, "4 Ways to Use AI in Your Business" (May 2026), he warns against leaving AI to technologists who don't understand your business. He says they tend to build generic, commoditized automations. His point is that owners who know their own operations spot the uses outsiders miss. He tells owners to build hands-on skills using YouTube and AI chatbots, and to understand the business from "cloud to dirt," meaning from high-level strategy down to the systems that run it. On X he wrote that this is a good moment because people in existing markets are "busy running their businesses rather than learning AI."

**3. Build a tool for your business, not a software company.** His 2022 episode "Why Starting A Software Company is a Terrible Idea" argues the field is crowded and most founders fail. The episode ends by telling you to stick to your own game and serve your customers. In 2026 he said "Use AI to increase leverage, not as a reason to pivot." So the app should make your existing business better. It shouldn't become a new business.

**4. Keep the thinking yourself.** He warns against letting AI make your judgment calls. Even if you build with AI, you decide what the app does and why.

**What I'd do:** Spend a few weekends building a rough version with AI coding tools. That's cheap, and it teaches you what you actually need. Then, if the app proves its value and starts handling customer data, payments, or real volume, pay a developer to make it solid. That second step is my own addition, not something Hormozi said. It fits his advice to put money only where the bottleneck is proven.
